key_insight: This paper shows that robotic policies often generalize poorly because they rely on biased instruction shortcuts instead of truly composing language factors like color, object, verb, size, and spatial relations. The authors propose a bias-aware diagnostic and data-collection strategy to expose these failures and improve compositional generalization.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of robots failing to follow novel combinations of instructions, especially when fine-tuned policies overfit to salient cues rather than learning the underlying meaning of each instruction component.
method: Introduces a diagnostic framework that breaks instructions into reusable factors such as verb, object, color, size, and spatial attribute.
Measures instruction factor bias to identify which components a policy over-relies on or ignores.
Uses bias-aware evaluation to localize generalization failures and guide more strategic data collection for robotic manipulation.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical way to evaluate whether a robot is actually understanding language or just exploiting shortcuts. It can improve data efficiency and make policy training more reliable for diverse real-world instructions.
visual_elements: A factor decomposition diagram showing an instruction split into color/verb/object/size/spatial parts.
A bias heatmap highlighting which instruction factors a policy attends to versus ignores.
A before-vs-after chart comparing standard evaluation with bias-aware evaluation.
An icon-based pipeline showing data collection, fine-tuning, diagnosis, and improved generalization.
paper_title: Scale Up Strategically: Learning Compositional Generalization via Bias-Aware Evaluation and Data Collection for Robotic Manipulation
paper_authors: Yu Qi, Zhang Ye, Xinyi Xu, Yuxuan Lu, Amitoj Sandhu
